title: Grandmother's warning about the reels and the new bass player in town
summary: His grandmother disapproved of clubs; he discovered bass in 1952 and was tolerated as the only bassist.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I see. So what would your grandmother have thought if you played a boogie woogie record in her house?

Oh my God she’d — I hear her today. She told me, she said, “Don’t ever go to those reels.” She called them “reels.” R-E-E-L-S, which meant the movies at the time. There was like that, what’s that, all of the oh Fats Navarro, people like that. Right? And apparently at the time, in Tulsa, you know, jazz music and rock, and rhythm & blues were just, you know, really the substance of entertainment for the entire community. And I think she had had an encounter with one of the people in the family that hung out at the clubs, contrary to going to her church. She told me, “Don’t you ever go to those reels or go to those places where they drink that alcohol and smoke those dirty cigarettes.” I was like that. That’s why when she got happy I wanted to get up out of there and run. I think about that often because if she knew that I was playing this kind of music she would be very uncomfortable with it.
I see. Yeah, this would have been late 40s, early 50s?
Yeah. This was like, oh let me see, I was, yeah, early 40s when I was with her. I was with her when I was seven or eight. And the early 50s was when I, — ‘52 was when I discovered the bass.

Yeah, the point is, I didn’t make, is that the moment I touched that bass, the first moment I touched that bass I was the new bass player in town ‘cause there were no bass players there. So you know I was tolerated until I could find my way.
